preview_text: อาการน้ำมูกไหลใสอย่างกะทันหันพร้อมกับหนาวสั่นคืออาการลมหนาวที่สามารถแก้ไขได้ภายในไม่กี่วันด้วยสมุนไพรที่เหมาะสม หยดเรื้อรังอย่างต่อเนื่องที่แย่ลงเมื่อเหนื่อยล้าหรือ ...
categories: ["ปัญหาจมูกและไซนัส"]
synonyms: ["Runny nose with clear discharge", "Clear watery nasal discharge", "Clear nasal discharge", "Clear thin nasal discharge", "Copious clear nasal discharge", "Slight runny nose with clear discharge", "Watery nasal discharge", "White watery nasal discharge", "White watery phlegm or nasal discharge", "White Nasal Discharge", "Runny Nose with Thin Discharge", "Nasal Congestion with Clear Watery Discharge", "Nasal congestion or runny nose with clear discharge", "Nasal congestion with clear runny discharge", "Stuffy nose with clear discharge"]
conventional_description:
In Western medicine, a runny nose with clear, watery discharge is often a symptom of allergic rhinitis (hay fever), viral upper respiratory infections (the common cold), or non-allergic triggers like cold air, spicy foods, or hormonal changes. It occurs when the nasal passages become inflamed, causing the mucous membranes to produce excess fluid.
Diagnosis is typically based on a history of symptoms, a physical exam, and sometimes allergy testing. While usually not serious, persistent clear nasal discharge can significantly affect quality of life and sleep.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatments include oral antihistamines, decongestant sprays or pills, and nasal corticosteroid sprays to reduce inflammation. For chronic allergic rhinitis, immunotherapy (allergy shots) may be recommended. Non-medication approaches like saline nasal rinses and avoiding known triggers are also first-line advice. These treatments effectively manage symptoms for many people but do not address why one person is more susceptible than another.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the nose is the opening of the Lung, and the Lung governs the body’s defensive Qi (Wei Qi) and the distribution of fluids. When Wind and Cold invade from the outside, they block the Lung’s ability to descend and disperse Qi. This constriction traps fluid in the upper body, and the nose - the Lung’s doorway - begins to leak a clear, watery discharge as the body tries to expel the pathogen.
This is the classic acute runny nose that comes on suddenly with chills and sneezing.
But a clear runny nose isn’t always an invasion. When it becomes chronic, the root often lies in a deficiency of the internal organs. Lung Qi Deficiency means the Lung lacks the strength to hold fluids in; the nose drips like a leaky faucet, and the person catches every cold that goes around.
Spleen Deficiency with Dampness creates an internal swamp - the Spleen fails to transform fluids, and the excess dampness rises to the nose as a persistent, clear trickle, often accompanied by bloating and loose stools. Kidney Yang Deficiency, the deepest of the patterns, leaves the entire body cold and unable to warm or control fluids, so the nose runs constantly, especially in cold weather.
This is why TCM never treats a runny nose as just a nose problem. The same clear discharge can be a brief skirmish at the body’s surface or a sign of a long-standing internal weakness. A practitioner differentiates by looking at the whole picture - the tongue, the pulse, the presence of chills or fatigue, the digestive symptoms - and then chooses a treatment that either expels the invader or rebuilds the body’s own defenses.
classical_quote: 「清涕者，由风寒伤于肺，肺气不和，津液壅塞，故鼻流清涕也。」
classical_translation: "Clear nasal discharge occurs when wind-cold injures the lungs, causing disharmony of lung qi and obstruction of fluids, hence the nose runs with clear discharge."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 29, Nasal Discharge 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner first asks when the runny nose began and what else is happening in the body. A sudden onset of clear watery nasal discharge (清涕, qīng tì) that arrives with chills, sneezing, and an aversion to wind points straight to Wind-Cold invading the Lungs. The tongue has a thin white coating and the pulse feels floating and tight (浮紧, fú jǐn), like a drum skin under the fingers. This picture is common at the start of a cold.
If the clear discharge appears briefly alongside a sore throat and a mild fever, the practitioner considers the early stage of Wind-Heat invading the Lungs. Here the tip of the tongue may be redder and the pulse is floating and rapid (浮数, fú shuò). The discharge is often thin and clear for only a short time before turning thicker and yellow. This pattern is less common for purely clear nasal discharge, but it can fool someone who only looks at the mucus color.
When the runny nose is chronic and the person catches colds easily, the focus shifts to deficiency. In Lung Qi Deficiency, the nose drips clear fluid off and on, and the person feels tired, has a weak voice, and sweats easily. The tongue is pale and the pulse is weak (弱, ruò).
Spleen Deficiency with Dampness adds digestive clues: poor appetite, bloating, loose stools, and a heavy sensation. The tongue is pale and puffy with tooth marks, and the pulse is soft (濡, rú). Both patterns share a slow, lingering quality that never truly goes away.
In long-standing cases, especially in older people, Kidney Yang Deficiency may be the root. The clear discharge is relentless, and the person feels deeply cold-cold limbs, aching lower back and knees, and a lack of vitality. The tongue is pale and swollen with a slippery white coat, and the pulse is deep and slow (沉迟, chén chí). The practitioner recognizes this as a deeper, constitutional chill that needs warming from the core.

patterns.symptoms: ["Sudden onset of clear watery nasal discharge", "Chills and aversion to cold more prominent than fever", "Absence of sweating", "Body aches and sore limbs", "Frequent sneezing", "Thin white watery phlegm or sputum"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold drafts and air conditioning, Cold raw foods and iced drinks, Overexertion and sweating, Sudden temperature drops, Dairy and greasy foods
patterns.better_with: Warm ginger or cinnamon tea, Staying warm and covered, Rest and sleep, Steam inhalation, Warm compress on face
patterns.why_this_happens: Wind and Cold invade the body through the skin and nose, lodging in the Lung’s defensive surface. The Cold constricts the pores and Lung Qi, disrupting the normal distribution of fluids. This trapped fluid overflows as a clear, watery nasal discharge, while the body’s effort to expel the pathogen triggers chills, sneezing, and body aches.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a thin white moist coating. Pulse: floating (fu) and tight (jin), easily felt at the surface.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Cold tightens the skin pores and Lung Qi, trapping fluids and causing chills. Warmth and gentle sweating open the pores, release the exterior, and allow Lung Qi to descend, stopping the runny nose. Rest conserves Qi, which is needed to expel the pathogen, while overexertion depletes Qi and lets the Cold penetrate deeper. Cold foods and drafts introduce more Cold, worsening the constriction, while warm foods and steam help the body’s Yang push out the invader.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Sip warm ginger and scallion tea to promote a light sweat and push out the cold. Keep your neck, upper back, and feet warm, and avoid exposure to drafts. Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid cold drinks, raw salads, and dairy, which can increase dampness. Rest is essential-do not exercise heavily while symptoms are acute.

patterns.symptoms: ["Clear watery nasal discharge that is chronic or recurrent", "Fatigue and tiredness", "Shortness of breath on exertion", "Spontaneous daytime sweating", "Sensitivity to wind and cold, catching colds easily", "Weak voice, reluctance to speak"]
patterns.worse_with: Overwork and exhaustion, Cold, windy weather, Cold, raw foods and icy drinks, Excessive physical exertion, Stress and worry
patterns.better_with: Rest and avoiding overexertion, Warmth, especially covering the chest and neck, Warm soups and stews, Ginger tea, Gentle exercise like walking
patterns.why_this_happens: When Lung Qi is weak, it cannot properly control the opening and closing of the pores and the nose. The Lung loses its ability to contain fluids, so thin, watery mucus leaks out as a clear runny nose. Because the defensive Qi is also weak, the body catches colds easily, and the discharge becomes chronic or recurrent.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body with possible teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: empty or weak, especially weak at the right Cun position (Lung).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Qi is easily depleted by overwork and stress, leaving the nose unguarded and prone to clear discharge. Cold and wind invade the weakened exterior, triggering more fluid leakage. Rest and warmth conserve Qi and help the Lung regain control of fluids. Warm foods and gentle movement gently build Qi without straining the body.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees, and avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks. Gentle exercise such as walking or Tai Chi helps build Qi without exhausting you. Keep your chest and neck covered in windy weather, and use a scarf to protect the back of the neck. Avoid overwork and get plenty of rest to allow the Lung Qi to recover.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is in charge of transforming food and fluids into usable Qi. When Spleen Qi is weak, it cannot properly manage water, and dampness accumulates internally. This dampness is heavy and tends to rise, overflowing upward to the nose and producing a persistent, clear, watery discharge. Because the root is a digestive weakness, the runny nose is often accompanied by bloating, loose stools, and a heavy, tired feeling in the body.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen body with teeth marks, white greasy coating, moist surface. Pulse: soggy (Ru) and slow (Huan), soft and weak, especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness directly weaken the Spleen's transformative fire, causing fluids to accumulate and rise to the nose. Raw, cold, and greasy foods add to this burden, making the discharge worse. Warm, cooked meals and ginger tea support the Spleen's Yang, helping it transform and transport fluids. Worry knots the Qi and impairs digestion, while gentle movement invigorates Qi circulation and helps dry dampness.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked meals like soups, congees, and stews. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen and create more dampness. Sip ginger tea to warm the digestive center. Gentle daily movement like walking helps circulate Qi and dry dampness. Do not overeat, and try to rest briefly after meals.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Kidneys are the root of Yang in the body, providing warmth to all organs, including the Lungs. When Kidney Yang is deficient, the Lungs lose their warming support and cannot properly control the nose and fluids. This allows clear, watery discharge to leak out continuously. Additionally, the Kidneys govern water metabolism; weak Yang fails to transform fluids, which then accumulate and rise upward as nasal discharge.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the rear (Chi) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire. Cold environments and cold foods directly weaken this fire, making the runny nose worse. Warmth, rest, and moxibustion help to stoke the fire, allowing the Kidneys to warm the Lungs and stop the discharge. Overwork and excessive activity drain Yang, leaving the body even colder.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep warm, especially the lower back and feet. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews with ginger and cinnamon. Avoid cold, raw foods and icy drinks. Moxibustion on the lower back and lower abdomen can be very helpful. Gentle exercise like Tai Chi or walking supports Yang without depleting it.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Wind-Heat invades from the outside, attacking the Lung's defensive surface. The Lung opens into the nose, so the initial fight between the body's Qi and the pathogen produces a thin, clear discharge. Because Heat quickly dries and condenses fluids, this clear stage is short-lived-soon the mucus turns yellow or thick.
The presence of Heat also brings a sore throat, thirst, and a feeling of warmth rather than chills, distinguishing this from a simple Wind-Cold invasion.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip with a thin yellow coating (may appear white at the very start). Pulse: floating (Fu) and rapid (Shu), especially at the right front position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen with a hot nature. Spicy foods and stuffy environments add more heat, fueling the invasion. Rest and cooling fluids help the body's defensive Qi to push the pathogen out and clear the heat, allowing the Lung to resume its normal function of controlling the nose and fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of lukewarm water and cooling herbal teas like chrysanthemum. Avoid spicy, greasy, or fried foods that add internal heat. Rest in a well-ventilated room and avoid drafts.

faqs.question: How does TCM tell if my runny nose is from a cold or allergies?
faqs.answer: TCM doesn’t separate colds from allergies in the same way Western medicine does. Instead, it looks at the whole picture. A sudden onset with chills, body aches, and a floating-tight pulse points to an external Wind-Cold invasion - what you might call a cold. A chronic, recurrent clear runny nose that flares up with fatigue, after eating, or in damp weather, with a weak pulse and a pale, swollen tongue, suggests an internal deficiency pattern, which often underlies what Western medicine labels allergic or vasomotor rhinitis. The treatment is chosen based on the pattern, not the label.
